notes_for_us: This game has two play spaces and the one-shape rule can only ship one. Classic mode is volume-open-air; Team mode is vehicle-deck, where the walkable surface is your own ship. Both shapes exist, both are correct, and the rule that keeps pipeline cost down forced the deck into notes. A mode-per-shape prompt is not a genre mix and nothing addresses it.

Weather is gameplay here - wind, rain and lightning change how ships move - and genre-choice has no channel for it at all. There is no sky or weather stream in the emit block, so the most-repeated environmental feature in a very long prompt is unroutable.

The prompt asks for a map generator, not a map: obstacles, weather and hazards assembled per battle. The handoff assumes one build, so 'these are the rules that generate the family' has nowhere to sit and reads downstream as a single fixed arena.

Step 0 handled a mostly-mechanics prompt cleanly, but mechanics came out with twelve unordered entries. That is a lot of weight on a field defined as pass-through, and nothing marks which of them have spatial consequences worth revisiting.

This is the padding case the brief describes, and the preset is not padding it dishonestly: Classic Obby is a reasonable read of 'obby'. But it means the shortest prompts get the highest ratio of invented content, and nothing in the emit block distinguishes a pick the user asked for from a pick the preset supplied.

'Rainbow' is a colour instruction with an ordering in it - red through violet, in sequence along the course - and the only field that can hold it is theme, which is a style vocabulary rather than a palette. It survived by being written into the path-track text, where a downstream reader has no reason to look for a global rule.

Step 4 says not to ask what the prompt already told you, and 'a rainbow obby' answers almost nothing, so every question here is live. The four-question cap bound before the holes ran out - course length, checkpoint density, and whether there is ground below all compete for the same slots.

notes_for_us: The same wall as the airship prompt, from the opposite direction: this game needs stage-runway and settlement-claimable, both in Roleplay's own typical-shapes line, and the exclusive-shape rule makes the apartments unbuildable. The genre note even says a dress-up game has no settlement - this one buys one, decorates it and invites friends over.

The deliverable is a set of maps with a redress rule, not a map. Ten votable venues and twenty rotating show themes are the product, and the handoff has one shape, one theme string and a P4 that says only 'more than one'. Nothing carries 'here are the ten, and here is what changes between them'.

Four thousand words of design document yielded about eight layout facts. Step 0 handled that exactly as written and it felt right - but the resulting mechanics array is twelve entries of unranked pass-through, and a reader downstream cannot tell that the twelve are the parts we deliberately did not build.

Roblox's round structure - lobby, reveal, phase, results - is Party and Casual's territory in the index, and this prompt is a round-based competition inside a roleplay genre. I did not name Party as a second genre because its options add nothing to this map, but the round loop is the game's actual skeleton and the classification does not show it.

notes_for_us: P6 validates platform spacing against default WalkSpeed and JumpHeight, and this prompt sets walk speed to 40 and adds a dash. Nothing in the handoff carries movement parameters, so the generator would build a course for a character that does not exist in this game - too-short gaps at best, an unvalidatable course at worst. The Vehicle Obby caveat recognises exactly this problem for cars and there is no equivalent for a buffed avatar, which is far more common.

Three distinctly themed stages inside one course have no representation anywhere. theme is one string, the option table has no stage or section division, and the genre notes explicitly say modern obbies are built this way - blended, hand-authored, one environment per stage. It survived as a count of 3 on path-track and a comma-separated theme string.

Numbers again land nowhere: platforms vanish 1 second after touch, walk speed is 40, there are exactly 3 levels. count took the level count because it happened to attach to a pick; the other two had no home.
